# Glacier backscatter time series

This tutorial follows the Aletsch glacier in the Swiss Alps through 2022, one
acquisition per month. It shows how backscatter changes with the seasons and
how to turn a stack of products into a time series for one site.


## Process one acquisition per month

The search covers a year of one burst footprint over the glacier. Keeping the
first acquisition of each month leaves twelve, which are downloaded and
processed into RTC backscatter at 20 m pixel size, in the burst's own UTM zone:

::: {#4df06e76 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from s1bursts import BurstCatalog, BurstProcessor, FileManager, RTCConfig, SearchQuery, TimeRange
from s1bursts.burst import BurstCollection

fm = FileManager("data/glacier")
catalog = BurstCatalog(fm)
bursts = catalog.search(SearchQuery(
    time_range=TimeRange("2022-01-01", "2022-12-31"),
    burst_id=30346, sub_swath="IW1", polarization="VV",
))

df = bursts.df.sort_values("date")
monthly = BurstCollection(df.groupby(df.date.dt.month).head(1))
print(f"{len(bursts)} acquisitions in 2022, {len(monthly)} selected")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
30 acquisitions in 2022, 12 selected
```
:::
:::


::: {#df86f3cb .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
catalog.download(monthly).raise_on_failure()
processor = BurstProcessor(fm)
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(
    monthly, crs="auto", config=RTCConfig(grid_spacing=20),
).raise_on_failure()
```
:::


## Map the glacier

The map shows the glacier in January and in May. The Great Aletsch Glacier
starts at Konkordiaplatz, where its tributaries meet near the top center, and
flows south-east, then south-west toward its tongue. In May the glacier and
much of the terrain around it are far darker than in January.

::: {#d1384600 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import rasterio
from rasterio.warp import transform_bounds
from rasterio.windows import from_bounds
from shapely.geometry import box

view = (7.95, 46.38, 8.15, 46.55)  # lon/lat bounds of the map
sample = box(8.065, 46.472, 8.072, 46.477)  # on the glacier below Konkordiaplatz
products = sorted(rtc.products, key=lambda p: p.date)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.8, 3.7), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, product in zip(axes, [products[0], products[4]]):
    with rasterio.open(fm.get_product_path(product)) as src:
        left, bottom, right, top = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", src.crs, *view)
        gamma0 = src.read(1, window=from_bounds(left, bottom, right, top, src.transform))
        x0, y0, x1, y1 = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", src.crs, *sample.bounds)
    extent = [v / 1000 for v in (left, right, bottom, top)]
    image = ax.imshow(10 * np.log10(gamma0), extent=extent, cmap="viridis", vmin=-25, vmax=0)
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x0 / 1000, y0 / 1000), (x1 - x0) / 1000, (y1 - y0) / 1000,
                               fill=False, edgecolor="white"))
    ax.set(title=f"{product.date:%d %B %Y}", xlabel="Easting (km)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)")
fig.colorbar(image, ax=axes, shrink=0.8, label="Gamma-0 (dB)")
plt.show()
```

![RTC backscatter around the Aletsch glacier in January and May 2022. The white rectangle is the sample area of the time series.](glacier-backscatter_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=737 height=366}
:::

## Extract a time series

The time series is the median backscatter within the sample rectangle on the
glacier. The median is taken in linear units and converted to decibels
afterwards, because averaging decibels gives a biased result.

::: {#1c9ae0a8 .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd
from rasterio.mask import mask
from rasterio.warp import transform_geom
from shapely.geometry import mapping

records = []
for product in products:
    with rasterio.open(fm.get_product_path(product)) as src:
        region = transform_geom("EPSG:4326", src.crs, mapping(sample))
        values, _ = mask(src, [region], indexes=1, crop=True, filled=False)
    valid = values.compressed()
    valid = valid[np.isfinite(valid)]
    records.append({"date": product.date, "gamma0_db": 10 * np.log10(np.median(valid))})
series = pd.DataFrame(records)
```
:::


::: {#e4826ea3 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.8, 3.3))
ax.plot(series.date, series.gamma0_db, "o-")
ax.set(xlabel="Acquisition date", ylabel="Median gamma-0 (dB)")
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
fig.autofmt_xdate()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Median RTC backscatter in the sample rectangle, one acquisition per month in 2022.](glacier-backscatter_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=656 height=303}
:::
:::


## Interpret the curve

Backscatter on the glacier stays near −10.5 dB from January to April, drops to
−18.5 dB on 9 May, and recovers to about −9 dB in August and September. Wet
snow is a likely cause of the drop: liquid water in the snowpack absorbs much
of the radar signal, as described in the
[Copernicus snow product manual](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/technical-library/product-user-manual-high-resolution-snow-products-europe/@@download/file).
From October, values settle around −12 to −13 dB.

A single curve does not establish the cause. Check the dates against
temperature, snowfall and snow-cover records before drawing conclusions, and
keep orbit, polarization and processing settings fixed across the series.
Monthly sampling can also miss short melt or snowfall events, since each month
contributes a single evening acquisition.

The [next tutorial](glacier-coherence.qmd) computes coherence for the same
burst.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
